draft.title: Gradient of an interval
card: Gradient measures how steep an interval is. Gradient \(=\) rise \(\div\) run, where the rise is the change up or down and the run is the change across.
Worked example: from \(A(1, 2)\) to \(B(5, 10)\), the rise is \(10 - 2 = 8\) and the run is \(5 - 1 = 4\). The gradient is \(\frac{8}{4} = 2\).
Going right, an interval that slopes up has a positive gradient. One that slopes down has a negative gradient, because the rise is negative.
A horizontal interval has rise 0, so its gradient is 0. A vertical interval has run 0, and you cannot divide by 0, so it has no gradient.

2.alt: An interval from A(1, 2) to B(5, 10) sloping up to the right. The run is 4 across and the rise is 8 up.

draft.remember: Gradient is rise over run: up is positive, down is negative.

a.q: An interval joins \(P(2, 9)\) and \(Q(6, 1)\). What is its gradient?
a.why: The rise is \(1 - 9 = -8\) and the run is \(6 - 2 = 4\), so the gradient is \(\frac{-8}{4} = -2\). The interval slopes down to the right, so the gradient is negative. Choosing \(2\) drops that sign.
a.clue: Which way does the interval go as you move right?

b.why: From \((3, 1)\) to \((3, 7)\) the run is \(3 - 3 = 0\), so the interval is vertical and has no gradient. The horizontal interval is tempting, but its rise is 0, so its gradient is 0, which is a gradient.
b.clue: Check which interval has a run of zero.
